q: What is a MAJOR swing level?
a: The top and the bottom of an IMPULSIVE move. An impulsive move is one that BREAKS previous structure. Minor swing levels are everything in between — and in a trending market you ignore them entirely.

q: When can you confirm a pullback low is a major swing level?
a: Only AFTER price breaks into new highs. Until then the pullback could keep going — you cannot know it was the bottom until a new high confirms it.

q: In an uptrend, what single rule tells you the trend is still intact?
a: Price stays ABOVE the most recent major swing low. No matter what happens in between (choppiness, consolidation), above that level = still an uptrend. This is why you draw horizontal lines at your major swing lows in an uptrend.

q: What is the FIRST hint that an uptrend may be ending?
a: A break and CLOSE below the most recent major swing low. It's a 'possible reversal' — you stop looking for long trades from that point.

q: What does the video call a 'one-two-three reversal move'?
a: The sequence that flips structure: the prior major swing level breaks, then price fails to reclaim it, then the next level breaks. Once the major support breaks after that, it is a downtrend — not a pullback.

q: How do you spot CONSOLIDATION, and what do you do about it?
a: You get a push to a major swing level, then a break and close back ABOVE the previous pullback high — while the prior low stays intact. Both sides now have a case = indecision. DO NOT TRADE. The video: 'this is when all of our losses occur.' Waits until one boundary level breaks.

q: Are support and resistance lines or zones?
a: ZONES. The video treats them as areas, not exact lines — e.g. combining two major swing levels that sit close together and splitting the difference between them.

q: How does the video define a pullback (its most objective rule)?
a: At least TWO candles, and real movement — not two tiny candles before a breakout. The author admits there is no fully objective rule for this; it comes with screen time.

q: At the very start, why do most day traders fail?
a: Two reasons: (1) no strategy they can stay consistent to, so they switch constantly or trade randomly; (2) they HAVE a strategy but it loses money, and they keep trading it until they're too frustrated to continue.

q: Does this strategy only work for forex or only for day trading?
a: No. The author uses it across ALL time frames and in the STOCK, FOREX and CRYPTO markets he trades.

q: RULE 1 of the strategy — what is it?
a: HIGHER TIME FRAME TREND. Align yourself with the trend of one time frame UP from the one you trade. Only take trades in that direction.

q: RULE 2 — what level do you use, and from which time frame?
a: The LAST MAJOR SWING LEVEL that was broken, taken from the higher time frame. Once a major swing level breaks, that is the level you watch for trend continuation.

q: RULE 3 — what is the entry trigger?
a: REJECTION at the zone, on the trading time frame. Bearish setup = DOUBLE TOP; bullish setup = DOUBLE BOTTOM.

q: Give the exact time-frame pairing ladder.
a: 5 min → check the 15 min. 15 min → the 1 hour. 1 hour → the 4 hour. 4 hour → the daily. Always exactly ONE time frame up; the author rarely goes higher than the daily.

q: Why does the strategy insist on the higher time frame at all?
a: To be on the correct SIDE of the market. The higher time frame tells you whether to be hunting longs or shorts. Rule 1 exists so rule 3's double top / double bottom lands in the direction of the bigger trend.

q: Define the ZONE for a bearish (double top) entry, precisely.
a: Between the HIGHEST BODIES of the previous swing high and the HIGHEST WICK of that same swing high. Wicks may touch it; bodies may close in it.

q: What is the ONE thing that must NOT happen inside the zone?
a: A CLOSE above the zone. A close above is continuation, not rejection — that's exactly what price had been doing before. Rejection requires price to be turned away.

q: After price touches the zone, what confirms the entry?
a: For a short: a RED candle showing sellers taking control. For a long: a GREEN candle showing buying pressure out of the zone.

q: What is the exact entry price?
a: The CLOSE of the rejection candle — equivalently, the OPEN of the next candle.

q: In the bullish recap on MSFT, what confirmed the double bottom?
a: Price pushed down, formed a bottom, formed a neckline, then RETESTED that area WITHOUT closing below it. That gave buying pressure — then a green candle, followed by an even bigger green candle, which is where the entry is taken.

q: What happens if price closes back above your zone before entry?
a: You are NOT interested in going short yet. The video shows exactly this: price broke through the high making a higher high, so no trade — the author waited for a push back into the level that then actually rejected.

q: Where does the STOP LOSS go?
a: BEYOND the extreme of the rejection: below the lowest low of the double bottom / rejection (for longs), or above the highest high (for shorts).

q: What extra buffer is added to the stop, and why?
a: The ATR (Average True Range). The author uses ATR(14) — the average movement of the last 14 candles — and places the stop that far beyond the swing low, to stay aligned with current market VOLATILITY.

q: Give the worked stop-loss example from the video.
a: MSFT long: swing low at 185.20, ATR 2.31 → stop placed 2.31 below the low, around 182.89.

q: Where is the TARGET?
a: Back at the PREVIOUS major swing level (previous resistance for longs, previous support for shorts). If there are two close together, pick the one further away / the sensible one — the video picks the slightly lower of two resistance levels so the target isn't over-ambitious.

q: What reward-to-risk ratio does the strategy target?
a: About 2:1. The demonstrated trades came out at 2.4:1 (AUD/CAD) and 2.3:1 (Litecoin).

q: What is the strategy's win rate, and why does it still make money?
a: 'A little bit less than 50%' / 'somewhere around 50%.' With a 2:1 reward:risk, ~50% is a POSITIVE EXPECTANCY — the edge only shows up over a large sample size.

q: Why is a risk management plan necessary if the strategy already has an edge?
a: Because a ~50% win rate means the next trade is close to a coin flip. If you risk your whole account on one trade you're gambling, not trading. Risk management keeps you 'chips and a chair at the poker table' long enough for the edge to play out.

q: What are the TWO jobs of the risk management plan?
a: (1) Stop you from blowing the account — it cuts that chance dramatically. (2) Keep you OUT OF YOUR EMOTIONS — fear and greed can't control decisions if the per-trade loss is small enough to handle comfortably.

q: Name the 'Triangle of Trading Success' — the three required skills.
a: 1) A STRATEGY you can stay consistent to that makes money over time. 2) A RISK MANAGEMENT PLAN that keeps you out of your emotions and keeps you from blowing the account. 3) TRADING PSYCHOLOGY / discipline.

q: What does trading psychology actually protect you from?
a: FOMO — buying because you missed a move; switching strategies; and REVENGE trading — going super aggressive right after a stop-out to win the money back. All are emotional mistakes that destroy the edge.

q: Why does making the per-trade loss SMALL matter emotionally?
a: You WILL have losing trades — the author does too. The point is for losses not to affect you emotionally, because emotional decisions wreck your statistical advantage and the whole money-making strategy with it.

q: What is the stated purpose of a rules-based strategy?
a: Consistency. A checklist beside your desk: once all the rules are ticked off, you enter. The video: 'a strategy that's rules based so you can stay consistent to it and it's proven to make money over time.'

q: Walk through the FULL pre-trade checklist in order.
a: 1) Identify the higher-time-frame trend (one TF up). 2) Find the LAST broken major swing level on that higher time frame — mark it as a ZONE. 3) Drop to the trading time frame. 4) Wait for price to pull back into the zone. 5) Look for a double top (short) / double bottom (long) with no close beyond the zone. 6) Wait for the red/green confirmation candle. 7) Enter at its close. 8) Stop = beyond the swing extreme ± ATR. 9) Target = previous major swing level. 10) Target ≈ 2:1.

q: What does the strategy say to do while price is chopping between two levels?
a: Nothing. Everything between the two boundary levels is consolidation and minor swing levels only. Do not trade until one level breaks and shows you the direction.

q: Recap the AUD/CAD trade from the video.
a: 5-minute chart, bearish TREND CONTINUATION. Price pulled back to the previously broken major swing level, showed rejection, and ran down to target. ~2.4:1 R:R, a couple of thousand dollars, in roughly one to two hours.

q: Recap the MSFT example used for the full recap.
a: 4-hour chart gives the trend and the last broken major swing level. Drop to the 1-hour to trade. Double bottom: push down, bottom, neckline, retest without closing below, green candle then a bigger green candle = entry. Stop below the low minus ATR(14) 2.31. Target the previous major swing high.

q: On the MSFT recap, which time frame is the TREND read on and which is TRADED?
a: Trend read on the 4-hour; traded on the 1-hour. The rule is always one time frame up from the trading chart.

q: Is this strategy limited to the examples shown (forex pairs, Litecoin, MSFT)?
a: No — the author explicitly states it works across all markets (stock, forex, crypto) and all time frames, and frames it as his favourite after 10 years of trading.

q: What does the video say about making this completely objective?
a: It can't be, and the author says so openly several times — particularly for identifying pullbacks and drawing major swing levels. That part is judgment honed by screen time, which is why the trend-identification lesson takes up most of the video.
